source.title: Is SGD a Bayesian sampler? Well, almost
source.authors: Chris Mingard; Guillermo Valle Pérez; J. Skalse; A. Louis

record.tranche_reason: The study tests partial label corruption and its effects on training and test error, but does not test completely random labels as in V1.
record.gate_note: The paper cites random-label fitting results from Zhang et al. (2016), but those cited results are not rows. It reports its own 20% corruption comparison; the 50% corruption discussion does not give a separate SGD training/test error result.
record.test_reason: The study directly trains a standard FCN with SGD on clean and partially randomized labels and measures training classification accuracy and test error, bearing on V4 using the original type of experiment.
record.authors_conclusion: The record accurately summarizes the corruption-specific conclusion: label corruption weakens posterior bias and Bayesian–SGD probability agreement. The paper's broader conclusion is that the untrained network's parameter–function map primarily determines inductive bias, with secondary effects from optimizer and hyperparameter choices.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures distributions over functions reached by optimizers and compares them with a Gaussian-process Bayesian posterior; it does not reproduce the original random-label experiment.
record.method_sensitivity: Label corruption changes the strength of the correlation between optimizer and Bayesian function probabilities.

fits_no_version.finding: Label corruption weakens the Bayesian posterior's preference for low-error functions and weakens agreement between Bayesian and SGD function probabilities.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Label corruption weakens inductive bias and the correspondence between Bayesian and optimizer sampling.

record.problems: The relevant corruption results cover a small test set (50 examples) and selected corruption levels, not a full progression to completely randomized labels. The reported test-error values have no stated uncertainty.
record.rows_left_out: No separate SGD error row is given for the 50% corruption mentioned in the Figure 6 discussion. The figure discussion compares Bayesian posterior probabilities and does not report a distinct SGD test-error value for that condition.

untested.parts: No explicit controlled result establishes zero training error and chance test error for completely randomized training labels with unchanged hyperparameters. Appendix E trains networks on generated labelings but varies hyperparameters and reports complexity rather than fitting error.
No comparison of training time or convergence slowdown across label-corruption levels.
No fitting experiments on shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels, or Gaussian-noise inputs.

The full corruption sweep, steady degradation across intermediate levels, and fully randomized chance-error endpoint are untested by the reported SGD error measurements. Convergence success rates are not reported.
No controlled removal or addition of weight decay, dropout, or data augmentation addressing random-label fitting and clean-label generalization.
No measurements of when real-label patterns and noisy labels are learned.

record.verdict_notes: The 50% corruption discussion concerns Bayesian function probabilities and supplies no separate SGD error result. Appendix E's generated-label complexity experiments do not establish V1's unchanged-hyperparameter fitting claim. Neither the limited corruption coverage nor discarded nonconvergent runs demonstrates a failure of V4.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not report its own result for completely random labels.
Training time or convergence slowdown as corruption increases is not reported.
Shuffled pixels, independently permuted pixels and Gaussian-noise inputs are not tested.
The paper reports an uncorrupted condition and a 20% corruption condition, but does not report a full sweep through all corruption levels or the fully randomized endpoint.
Weight decay, dropout and data augmentation are not tested for this claim.
The study does not compare the timing or order of learning real-label patterns and noise.

rows.subject: 2-layer 1024 node wide FCN
rows.operation_detail: Train on uncorrupted binarised MNIST until 100% training accuracy; measure test error.
rows.note: The paper states the network is trained to zero training error; this is the uncorrupted reference condition.
rows.check: The value and conditions are correct. This is the clean-label control; 2.64% is mean test error across retained runs. Runs failing to reach 100% training accuracy are discarded.

source_check.locator_found: Figure 19(a), p. 56; Sections 3.1.2 and 3.3; Appendix A.1.1.

rows.subject: 2-layer 1024 node wide FCN
rows.operation_detail: Train on MNIST with 20% of training labels randomized until 100% training accuracy; measure test error.
rows.note: The reported optimizer test error increases relative to the uncorrupted condition; the training procedure stops at 100% training accuracy.
rows.check: The value and conditions are correct. Write the sample count as 10^5, not 105. The 13.4% mean test error describes retained zero-training-error runs; the paper does not report the fraction of attempted runs that converged.

source_check.correct: Sample count n = 10^5, not 105. Mean SGD test error is 13.4%, compared with 2.64% without corruption, conditional on reaching zero training classification error.
source_check.locator_found: Figure 19(a,c), p. 56; Figure 6 caption, p. 19; Section 3.1.2, footnote 4; Appendix A.1.1.

relationships.reason: R1 and R2 show zero training classification error with mean test error increasing from 2.64% to 13.4%, consistent with fitting corrupted labels while retaining generalizable signal.

tranche.reason: The relevant experiment uses the original method and measures: train a standard network with randomized training labels, measure perfect training classification fit and test error. The additional Bayesian comparison does not change that experiment.

source_check.notes: Nonconvergent runs are discarded, so perfect training fit is conditional on run retention. The fixed test set contains only 50 examples; the authors explicitly note sensitivity to a difficult image.
